newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Improved output extends St.Helena mine life.
newsitem.headline: Improved output extends St.Helena mine life.

text.p: St. Helena Gold Mines Ltd said on Thursday that improved productivity under a new wage scheme had extended the mine's lifespan by an extra 11 years and could prolong it still further.

St.Helena general manager Joe Hardy told analysts and reporters on a mine visit that the new bonus-orientated wage scheme had lowered the pay limit of the mine to 800 centimetre grammes a tonne (cmg/t) of ore in February 1997, from 1,200 cmg/t in February last year.

The pay limit is the point at which the mine can extract gold profitably. The reduction of the pay limit means the mine's life at current mining rates has been lengthened from seven years to 18.7 years, Hardy said.
Hardy said the mine -- which only a year ago was faced with closure -- aimed to reduce the pay limit further to 600 cmg/t, which would give it a 21-year lifespan.
Hardy said the new bonus scheme was tied to production levels, safety and efficiency and had upped the productivity of the workforce.
"Without more flexible bonuses there was no incentive for them (the miners)," Hardy said.
Tonnes of ore milled a month had also increased over the same period from 47,000 to 78,000.

The new bonus scheme -- which includes penalties for inefficiencies such as explosives wastage -- replaces a scheme where the maximum bonus was 230 rand a month. Now miners can earn bonuses of more than 3,000 rand a month.
St.Helena is managed by South African mining house Gengold Ltd.
In the quarter to end-December 1996 the mine produced 1,400 kg of gold against 1,168 kg in the preceding quarter.
The mine has retrenched heavily over the past few years, but Hardy said there would be no further job losses.
"We will not retrench. We cannot retrench, it would destroy people's morale," he said.
